q: The benefit of treating localised prostate cancer in a given man should mainly be judged by:
o: Risk of prostate-cancer death compared with competing causes of death over time
e: Ten years of life expectancy is only a rough guide. A man with aggressive disease may benefit even with a shorter life expectancy.
s: Ch 153 Management strategies for localised prostate cancer

q: The tool built to predict 10-year mortality from other causes in men with prostate cancer, using their comorbidities, is:
e: 10-year mortality from other causes rose from 10% at score 0 to 99% at score 10. In practice, doctors judge life expectancy by age more than by comorbidity.
s: Ch 153 Management strategies for localised prostate cancer

q: SPCG-4 (prostatectomy vs watchful waiting) showed a survival benefit for surgery, but its main limitation is:
o: High death rates from other causes
Enrolment mainly before the PSA era (about 90% palpable tumours)
e: Its results do not translate directly to screen-detected cancers.
s: Ch 153 Management strategies for localised prostate cancer

q: The main limitation of PIVOT is:
o: High death rates from other causes (about 40% dead by 10 years, only about 5% from prostate cancer)
e: At 19.5 years, surgery gave no significant all-cause benefit overall, but did benefit intermediate-risk men (absolute risk reduction 14.5%).
s: Ch 153 Management strategies for localised prostate cancer

q: ProtecT showed no difference in prostate-cancer mortality at 10 years mainly because:
o: Most men had low-risk (GG1, low PSA) disease, so few events occurred (about 1% mortality)
e: Metastases were more frequent with active monitoring. The 15-year update (2023) confirmed similar low mortality, about 3%.
s: Ch 153 Management strategies for localised prostate cancer; ProtecT 15-y (2023)

q: The 2005 ISUP modification of Gleason grading:
o: Reclassified all cribriform glands as pattern 4 and dropped patterns 1–2, shifting scores upwards
e: This makes it harder to compare older cohorts with modern ones. Grade groups came later (2014 ISUP).
s: Ch 153 Management strategies for localised prostate cancer

q: On prostate MRI, seminal vesicle invasion is characterised by a high:
e: When MRI calls seminal vesicle invasion it is usually right, but it misses focal extraprostatic extension (low sensitivity and NPV). The ADC value is the MRI parameter that best predicts outcome.
s: Ch 153 Management strategies for localised prostate cancer

q: The main concern in a man with Grade Group 1 cancer is:
o: Higher-grade cancer already present but missed at biopsy (about 25%)
e: True biological upgrading occurs in only 1–2% a year. GG1 cancer does not metastasise. Microfocal cancer is present in 50–60% of middle-aged men.

q: Which factor increases the risk of coexistent higher-grade cancer in a man on surveillance?
o: More positive cores or greater core involvement
e: Plan a confirmatory biopsy within 1 year, targeting under-sampled areas.

q: About what proportion of men on active surveillance are treated by 10 years?
e: 20–30% are treated by 5 years. Delaying treatment does not reduce its effectiveness.

q: Which is the most reliable trigger for intervention during surveillance?
e: PSA kinetics and volume increases have not reliably predicted adverse outcomes.

q: A man on surveillance should switch to watchful waiting when:
o: His estimated life expectancy falls below about 5–7 years
He has been stable for 10 years
e: A man who refuses biopsy can still be followed actively, for example with MRI.

q: According to the chapter, which feature should automatically exclude a man from surveillance?
e: A small amount of pattern 4 may be over-grading. Guidelines now also allow carefully selected favourable intermediate-risk men onto surveillance.

q: The standard follow-up schedule for active surveillance in the chapter is:
o: Confirmatory biopsy within 1 year, PSA every 6 months, and repeat biopsy every 3–5 years
e: MRI with targeted biopsy may replace serial systematic biopsy in very low-risk men. Higher-risk men still need systematic biopsies.

q: Which statement on the biology of Gleason pattern 3 is correct?
o: It has a high mutation burden
It is rare in Asian men
Most oncogenic pathways are intact (normal) in pattern 3 but altered in patterns 4–5
e: Microfocal pattern 3 occurs with age in all races.

q: The prostate's main arterial supply is the:
e: Accessory (aberrant) pudendal arteries from the obturator or vesical arteries can supply the penis and should be preserved.

q: The neurovascular bundles lie:
o: Between the prostatic fascia and the levator fascia (lateral pelvic fascia)
e: The capsular arteries and veins are the visible landmark for the cavernous nerves. The pelvic plexus is parasympathetic, from S2–S4.

q: Passive urinary control after radical prostatectomy depends mainly on:
o: The striated urethral sphincter (slow-twitch, fatigue-resistant fibres)
e: The striated sphincter and levator ani are supplied by the pudendal nerve. Post-prostatectomy incontinence is usually intrinsic sphincter deficiency.

q: The puboprostatic ligaments should be divided:
o: Only superficially, enough to expose the junction of the prostatic apex and dorsal vein complex, keeping the pubourethral part
e: The pubourethral component anchors the striated sphincter to the pubis.

q: Brisk bleeding from a partly divided dorsal vein complex is best managed by:
o: Dividing the complex completely over the urethra and oversewing the end
e: Pulling on a partly divided complex keeps the veins open and worsens bleeding.

q: The most common site of a positive surgical margin at open prostatectomy is:
o: The apex, during division of the dorsal vein complex and sphincter
e: Next most common are posterior, then posterolateral. Sew the cut dorsal vein edges in a V so the neurovascular bundles are not pulled forward.

q: The final decision on whether to preserve a neurovascular bundle can be made:
o: After the prostate is removed, if there is too little tissue covering the posterolateral surface
e: Other signs that a bundle must be excised: induration of the lateral pelvic fascia, or a bundle fixed to the prostate. Avoid thermal energy near the bundles.

q: After radical prostatectomy, a patient needs acute transfusions for hypotension. Best approach:
o: Re-explore and evacuate the pelvic haematoma
e: Leaving the haematoma raises the risk of bladder neck contracture and incontinence.

q: A rectal injury recognised during radical prostatectomy is best managed by:
o: Two-layer repair with omentum placed between the repair and the anastomosis
e: The omentum reduces the risk of a rectourethral fistula. Avoid rectal suppositories or manipulation after surgery.

q: Which statement about sparing the bladder neck or seminal vesicles is correct, according to the chapter?
o: Neither has been shown to improve continence, potency, margins or stricture rates
e: Complete seminal vesicle excision is recommended for cancer control. About 15–20% of men develop a (usually indirect) inguinal hernia afterwards.

q: Salvage radical prostatectomy after radiotherapy, according to the chapter:
o: Is first-line for any PSA rise
Is for clearly localised disease; about 50% incontinence, 24% stricture, near-universal ED; rectal injury is the complication that has improved most with experience
e: About 45% have recurrence at 5 years.

q: Sural nerve interposition grafting when a neurovascular bundle must be sacrificed:
o: Is placed in reversed orientation; in a randomised trial it gave no potency benefit over no graft
e: Recovery of erections depends on age, potency before surgery and nerve sparing (for example, 42% at 3 months and 73% at 1 year in one series). Defer surgery 6–8 weeks after biopsy and 3 months after TURP.

q: Blood loss is low in laparoscopic and robotic prostatectomy mainly because:
o: The dorsal vein is not divided
e: Transfusion should be below 2%. Taking the pedicles early and the dorsal vein late (antegrade approach) also reduces bleeding.

q: Compared with the transperitoneal approach, extraperitoneal robotic prostatectomy:
o: Avoids handling the bowel, which helps after extensive abdominal surgery
e: Margin rates do not differ by approach. Margins fall as the surgeon gains experience.

q: Prolonged CO₂ pneumoperitoneum in steep Trendelenburg mainly risks:
o: Hypercarbia, acidosis and oliguria, plus corneal oedema, raised intraocular pressure and nerve compression injury
e: Pad all pressure points carefully.

q: An iatrogenic positive apical margin in robotic prostatectomy often arises from:
o: A posterior (or anterior) lip of apex protruding beneath the urethra
e: Check the shape of the apex before dividing the posterior urethra.

q: Rectal injury during robotic prostatectomy is best avoided by:
o: Sharp, complete incision of the posterior layer of Denonvilliers fascia and antegrade release of the rectum from the prostate
e: Rectal injury is more common in salvage surgery, which belongs in experienced, high-volume centres.

q: The only absolute contraindication to minimally invasive prostatectomy listed in the chapter is:
o: An uncorrectable bleeding disorder (or being unfit for general anaesthesia)
e: Large glands, a median lobe, obesity and prior TURP or radiotherapy are best avoided early in a surgeon's experience, but are not absolute contraindications.

q: Which statement on robotic prostatectomy outcomes, according to the chapter, is correct?
o: Cancer control is worse than open surgery
Cancer outcomes equal open surgery, but at least 20% of men are not pad-free and about 5% have severe incontinence
e: Bladder neck stricture should be under 5% and machine failure under 0.5%. Discharge within 24 hours and return to activity by 3 weeks are typical.

q: Which statement on pelvic lymph node dissection is correct?
o: Minimally invasive dissection yields fewer nodes than open
Recommended for intermediate/high risk or nomogram nodal risk above 5%; clipping lymphatics reduces lymphoceles
e: The therapeutic value of an extended dissection is still debated.

q: Which is unfavourable intermediate-risk disease?
e: Unfavourable intermediate risk includes primary pattern 4 (GG3) or more than one intermediate-risk factor. 4+4 is high risk, and so is cT3a.

q: Phoenix (RTOG-ASTRO) biochemical failure after radiotherapy is defined as:
e: The older ASTRO definition was three consecutive rises. A nadir below 0.5 ng/mL predicts success, and the nadir is the strongest predictor of outcome.

q: A sexually active 53-year-old's PSA falls to 1.2 at 12 months after I-125 brachytherapy, then rises to 3.2 at 18 months. Best step:
o: Likely benign PSA bounce: review dosimetry, check PSA every 3 months, biopsy if not falling by 30 months
e: Bounces occur in up to 65% of men under 55 and can mimic distant failure. A biopsy after radiotherapy can be interpreted reliably about 30 months after treatment.

q: In NCIC/MRC and SPCG-7, adding radiotherapy to ADT for high-risk or locally advanced disease improved:
e: For example, 10-year mortality was 39.4% with ADT alone vs 29.6% with ADT plus radiotherapy in SPCG-7.

q: Radium-223 (ALSYMPCA) was approved in 2013 for:
o: Metastatic CRPC with bone metastases; overall survival
e: It is an alpha emitter that spares the marrow compared with the beta emitter strontium-89.

q: Which isotope half-life pairing is correct?
o: I-125: about 60 days; Pd-103: about 17 days
e: Typical prescribed doses: I-125 140–160 Gy, Pd-103 110–125 Gy, IMRT 75–79 Gy. Brachytherapy has a steep dose fall-off within millimetres.

q: Proton beam therapy's physical advantage, and its clinical status per the chapter:
o: Bragg peak with sharp dose fall-off beyond range; no proven clinical advantage over IMRT
e: Hypofractionated regimens have since become standard (CHHiP, PACE-B).

q: Late toxicity after conformal EBRT, according to the chapter:
o: About 50% of potent men are impotent at 5 years; about 10% have some rectal bleeding
e: Earlier TURP increases early urinary toxicity. Waiting 6–8 weeks after TURP reduces stricture and incontinence.

q: Which statement about mpMRI before focal therapy is FALSE?
o: It accurately sizes tumours for ablation margins
It improves detection of anterior tumours
e: MRI underestimates tumour volume by 5–30%. Its 10–15% miss rate means systematic biopsy is still needed.

q: For complete cell kill, focal cryotherapy should reach:
e: Slow thawing kills more cells. On ultrasound, the ice ball appears as a hyperechoic rim with acoustic shadowing.

q: How does HIFU destroy prostate tissue?
o: Coagulative necrosis from focused heating to at least 55 °C
e: The transrectal probe reaches posterior lesions best. Anterior lesions are harder because energy is lost passing through tissue and swelling develops. Whole-gland HIFU needs retreatment in 29–38% of men.

q: Which ablation method is NON-thermal?
e: VTP uses near-infrared light to activate a photosensitiser in the blood, producing reactive oxygen species. IRE opens pores in cell membranes and spares connective tissue.

q: Level 1 evidence for focal therapy (Azzouzi, padeliporfin VTP vs active surveillance in low-risk disease) showed:
o: Less progression (28% vs 58%) and more negative biopsies at 2 years
e: No randomised trial has compared focal therapy with radical treatment.

q: The recommended way to assess success after focal therapy is:
o: MRI with targeted biopsy of the treated area, plus systematic biopsy of the untreated gland
e: PSA is less useful because untreated tissue keeps producing it. ICUD 2015: targeted biopsy at 3–6 months, then MRI and systematic biopsy at 1–2 and 5 years.

q: The 'index lesion' concept supporting focal therapy is based on all EXCEPT:
o: Metastases are usually polyclonal from many foci
Satellite tumours are usually small (under 0.5 mL) and low grade
The index lesion usually determines grade and stage
It contributes most of the tumour volume
e: Genetic studies suggest metastatic or lethal disease usually arises from one clone (monoclonal).
